facts.claim: In the German movement, many participants sought representative government and national unity. Their goals varied.
Delegates to the first German National Assembly met in Frankfurt in 1848 and worked on a constitution for a united Germany.
The assembly debated and drafted a constitution for a unified German state. Its project did not establish the empire later proclaimed in 1871.
Some German nationalists supported constitutional rights and unity together, while others favoured different political arrangements.
Frederick William IV declined the offer in 1849. The assembly could draft a constitution, but it could not compel German rulers to accept its settlement.

The Frankfurt Assembly’s constitutional project failed. The later empire was created under Prussian hegemony, following wars against Denmark, Austria and France; Austria was outside the new German state.
Giuseppe Mazzini founded Young Italy, which promoted a united Italian nation and republican ideas.
Piedmont-Sardinia, ruled by the House of Savoy, became the main state platform for the unification process.
Cavour was a leading statesman of Piedmont-Sardinia. His diplomacy and political strategy helped expand the kingdom and advance unification.
Garibaldi’s volunteer force landed in Sicily and helped bring the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies under the unification movement. Rome joined Italy later.
Cavour served as prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia. Mazzini founded Young Italy, while Garibaldi led the Expedition of the Thousand.
The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861, with Victor Emmanuel II as its king.
Garibaldi’s expedition took place in 1860. The kingdom was proclaimed in 1861, and Rome was incorporated in 1870.
Italian forces entered Rome in 1870, and the city became part of the Kingdom of Italy. The kingdom had been proclaimed in 1861.
The expedition helped bring the south into the movement before the kingdom was proclaimed. Venetia joined in 1866, and Rome in 1870.
Victor Emmanuel II, formerly king of Piedmont-Sardinia, became king of Italy when the kingdom was proclaimed in 1861.
Mazzini’s Young Italy promoted a republican vision. Cavour worked through the government of Piedmont-Sardinia and diplomatic alliances.
Garibaldi’s campaign changed control in the south, while Cavour’s government helped bring those gains into the expanding Kingdom of Italy. Their methods and political aims were not identical.
Prussia fought Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870–71. The German Empire was proclaimed in January 1871.
After defeating Austria in 1866, Prussia organised the northern German states in the North German Confederation. Austria remained outside it.
The Zollverein encouraged economic cooperation by reducing customs barriers among participating German states; it did not itself create a single German nation-state.
Prussia took the leading role in the customs union. Austria remained outside the Zollverein, strengthening Prussia’s economic influence among German states.
The Zollverein linked many German states economically and increased Prussia’s influence, but political unification came later.
The Frankfurt Assembly attempted a parliamentary and constitutional solution. The 1871 empire emerged through Prussian-led wars and political agreements.
Prussia and Austria defeated Denmark in 1864; Prussia defeated Austria in 1866 and formed the North German Confederation; the empire was proclaimed in 1871 after the war with France.
The Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 preceded the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles in January 1871.
After 1866, Prussia organised the North German Confederation. Austria was excluded from this Prussian-led arrangement.
The new German Empire was organised under Prussian leadership and did not include Austria.
Prussia’s victory ended Austria’s leading role in German affairs and was followed by the North German Confederation.
Bismarck was Prussia’s minister-president and a central political strategist in the process that produced the Prussian-led German Empire.
The Compromise created the Austro-Hungarian Dual Monarchy, with Austria and Hungary retaining separate governments in important domestic matters under the same monarch.
The Habsburg ruler was emperor of Austria and king of Hungary, reflecting the monarchy’s dual structure.
Foreign affairs and common military affairs were shared responsibilities, while Austria and Hungary retained separate institutions for many internal matters.
The Compromise accommodated Hungarian demands through a dual monarchy, but other nationalities within the empire did not all receive equivalent self-government.
The 1867 settlement addressed the relationship between Austria and Hungary, but it did not satisfy the political aspirations of every nationality in the empire.
Francis Joseph I remained the common monarch after the Compromise, ruling as emperor of Austria and king of Hungary.
The settlement joined Austria and Hungary under one monarch and shared selected responsibilities, while leaving separate political institutions in each half.
The compromise reorganised the Habsburg monarchy around Austria and Hungary; it did not grant equivalent political arrangements to all its national communities.
As Ottoman authority weakened in parts of southeastern Europe, different national movements sought greater autonomy or independent statehood. Their aims and outcomes varied.
As Ottoman authority weakened in parts of southeastern Europe, national movements sought greater autonomy or independent statehood.
The 1878 Treaty of Berlin recognised Serbia’s independence, while also revising territorial arrangements in the Balkans.
The Treaty of Berlin recognised the independence of Serbia and Romania, among other changes to the region’s political map.
The treaty authorised Austria-Hungary to occupy and administer Bosnia and Herzegovina, even though the territory formally remained under Ottoman sovereignty at that time.

The Congress revised the larger Bulgarian settlement proposed earlier: a smaller autonomous principality was created north of the Balkans, while Eastern Rumelia had a separate status under Ottoman sovereignty.
The Austro-Hungarian Compromise preceded the Russo-Ottoman war settlement at San Stefano; the Congress of Berlin later revised that settlement in 1878.
The treaty recognised Romania’s independence and assigned it territory in Dobruja while also addressing Bessarabia’s transfer to Russia.
The Congress revised the San Stefano settlement and set new arrangements for Bulgaria, Serbia, Romania, Montenegro, and Bosnia-Herzegovina.
The congress was a great-power diplomatic meeting. Its decisions affected Balkan populations and borders but did not mean every local national demand had been settled.
The German Empire was formed under Prussian leadership; Balkan political changes followed different national struggles and diplomatic settlements involving European powers.
The Compromise created the Dual Monarchy in 1867; the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871; the Congress of Berlin met in 1878.
Mazzini founded Young Italy and promoted a united Italy with a republican form of government.
Garibaldi’s campaign helped overthrow Bourbon rule in Sicily and southern Italy; those gains were then incorporated into the expanding Kingdom of Italy.
Cavour used the resources and diplomacy of Piedmont-Sardinia to advance Italian unification.
Victor Emmanuel II became king when the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861. Rome joined the kingdom in 1870, completing a later stage of unification.
Young Italy promoted national unity and republican ideas; its programme differed from Cavour’s state-centred strategy.
The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861 under Victor Emmanuel II; Rome and Venetia joined later.
Rome was incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy in 1870, completing a major stage of the unification process.
Garibaldi’s military campaign changed control in the south; the Piedmont-Sardinian government then incorporated these gains into the expanding Italian kingdom.
The Italian process combined Mazzini’s and Garibaldi’s popular movements with Cavour’s statecraft; German unification followed a Prussian-led path involving wars and agreements.
Italy was proclaimed in 1861, the North German Confederation followed the 1866 war, Rome joined Italy in 1870, and the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871.
